lessons.title: dbt Fundamentals: What Problem Does It Solve?

slots.practicalActivity: Before touching dbt itself, write down (in your own words) the transformation steps you'd hand-write in raw SQL to turn a raw orders table into a clean, tested customers summary — then read back over it and circle every step that's really 'the same SQL copy-pasted with small edits,' since that repetition is exactly what dbt exists to remove.
slots.deliverable: A short written note listing the raw-SQL transformation steps you'd need without dbt, with the repeated/copy-pasted steps circled.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free dbt Cloud account (or install dbt Core locally with `pip install dbt-snowflake`), then run `dbt init` and open the generated project folder. Match every top-level item (models/, macros/, tests/, seeds/, dbt_project.yml, packages.yml) to what it's for, and open dbt_project.yml to find the `profile:` line.
slots.deliverable: A real dbt project scaffold on disk (or in dbt Cloud) with a written one-line note on what each top-level folder holds.

slots.practicalActivity: Connect your dbt project to your own Snowflake account (reusing the account and warehouse from the Snowflake course if you have one) by filling out profiles.yml or dbt Cloud's connection screen with your account, role, warehouse, and database, then run `dbt debug` to confirm the connection before running `dbt run` on the default example models.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed `dbt debug` success message and a terminal/screenshot showing `dbt run` building the starter models into Snowflake.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one raw table you have access to in Snowflake (reuse AdventureWorks/Northwind data from the Snowflake course, or your own raw schema), write a real sources.yml declaring it with database/schema/table, then build a staging model that selects from it with `{{ source(...) }}`, renaming and type-casting at least 3 columns.
slots.deliverable: A working sources.yml plus one staging model (e.g. stg_orders.sql) that builds successfully with `dbt run --select stg_orders`.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a second staging model on a related raw table, then write a new model under models/marts/ that joins both staging models together using two `{{ ref(...) }}` calls (not hardcoded table names) — mirroring the customers.sql walkthrough's min/max/count pattern over orders.
slots.deliverable: A new model file using two ref() calls that builds successfully, with its row count and a few sample rows confirmed via a plain SELECT in Snowflake.

lessons.title: Model Materializations: View, Table, Incremental & Ephemeral

slots.practicalActivity: Take the model you just built and explicitly set its materialization to `table` in a config() block, run `dbt run`, then switch it to `view` and rerun, comparing the Snowflake object type each time. Reorganize your models/ folder into staging/ and marts/ subfolders matching this chapter's convention.
slots.deliverable: One model whose materialization you've toggled between view and table (confirmed in Snowflake's object browser), inside a reorganized staging/marts folder structure.

slots.practicalActivity: Clean up your staging models so each one is strictly one-to-one with its raw source (renamed columns, cast types, no joins or aggregations), then build one intermediate model that combines two of those staging models into something neither one is alone — e.g. orders joined to order line items before anything reaches a mart.
slots.deliverable: At least 2 clean one-to-one staging models and 1 intermediate model combining them, all building successfully with `dbt run`.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the mart that sits on top of your intermediate model, naming it after the business entity it represents (e.g. orders, not orders_per_day or finance_orders), and denormalize deliberately by adding 1-2 computed columns a dashboard would otherwise have to derive itself (e.g. an is_large_order boolean).
slots.deliverable: One entity-named mart model with at least one deliberately denormalized computed column, materialized as a view.

lessons.title: The Layering Philosophy: Why Three Layers

slots.practicalActivity: Draw (on paper or in any diagramming tool) your project's current staging-to-intermediate-to-marts lineage as boxes and arrows, labeling each box source-conformed or business-conformed, then write 2-3 sentences explaining why skipping the intermediate layer and joining straight from staging to marts would have made your mart's SQL harder to read.
slots.deliverable: A hand-drawn or digital lineage diagram of your 3-layer project, plus a short written justification for keeping the intermediate layer.

slots.practicalActivity: Add `unique` and `not_null` tests to your mart's primary key column and a `relationships` test on a foreign key pointing at its dimension, then write one singular test in tests/ encoding a business rule the generic tests can't express (e.g. order_total should never be negative). Run `dbt test`, then deliberately break one assertion and rerun to see a real FAIL line.
slots.deliverable: A schema.yml with 3 generic tests plus 1 singular SQL test, and a terminal showing both a passing `dbt test` run and one deliberately triggered FAIL.

slots.practicalActivity: Write real `description:` fields for your mart model and every one of its columns in schema.yml, then run `dbt docs generate` and `dbt docs serve` to view the generated documentation site, clicking into your mart's lineage graph node to confirm your descriptions and tests both show up.
slots.deliverable: A schema.yml with model- and column-level descriptions, and a screenshot or local browser view of the generated dbt Docs site showing your mart's page.

lessons.title: Exposures: Connecting Models to Downstream BI

slots.practicalActivity: Add an `exposures.yml` declaring a dashboard (real or planned, e.g. in Power BI) that depends on your mart, naming its owner and the models it depends on, then regenerate dbt Docs and confirm the exposure shows up as its own node, connected to your mart, in the lineage graph.
slots.deliverable: A working exposures.yml entry visible as a connected node in the dbt Docs lineage graph after `dbt docs generate`.

slots.practicalActivity: Testing & docs drill: without re-reading the lessons, add a full test suite to a mart you haven't tested yet (not_null, unique, relationships, one singular test), write complete schema.yml descriptions for it, and generate dbt Docs — treat a 100% green `dbt test` run plus a fully documented model page as the pass/fail bar for this drill.
slots.deliverable: A second mart model with a complete test suite (all green) and full schema.yml documentation, confirmed in a fresh dbt Docs build.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a small CSV of static reference data (e.g. a region or status lookup table) under seeds/, run `dbt seed` to load it, and reference it with `{{ ref(...) }}` in an existing model. Then configure a snapshot on a dimension table that changes over time, run `dbt snapshot`, change a source row, and rerun to see the history captured.
slots.deliverable: A working seed loaded via `dbt seed` and referenced in a model, plus a snapshot table showing at least 2 historical versions of one changed row after a second `dbt snapshot` run.

slots.practicalActivity: Convert one of your fact-style models to `materialized='incremental'` with a `unique_key` and an `is_incremental()` filter on a timestamp column, set `incremental_strategy='merge'` explicitly, then update one existing source row's non-key column and rerun to confirm the target table shows the updated value with no duplicate row.
slots.deliverable: An incremental model using the merge strategy, with before/after row counts proving an updated source row produced zero duplicates in the target table.

slots.practicalActivity: Switch your incremental model's strategy to `append`, repeat the same update-and-rerun test from the previous slot, and observe the duplicate row it produces — then fix it by running `dbt run --full-refresh` on that model and switching the strategy back to merge.
slots.deliverable: A documented before/after comparison (screenshot or written note with row counts) showing the duplicate caused by `append` and the clean result after `--full-refresh` with `merge` restored.

slots.practicalActivity: Incremental lab: build one brand-new incremental model from scratch on a different source table, choosing the strategy yourself (merge, delete+insert, or append) based on whether its rows can be updated after arrival, and write a one-paragraph justification for your choice before testing it with a real update-and-rerun cycle.
slots.deliverable: A second original incremental model with a written strategy justification, verified correct across two consecutive `dbt run` executions.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a `{% for %}` loop in a model that generates one summed column per value in a short list (e.g. one column per order status), confirm it with `dbt compile`, then extract that same idea into a real custom macro under macros/ with at least one default-valued argument and call it from two different models.
slots.deliverable: One model using a Jinja for-loop and one custom macro (with a default argument) called from at least two models, both confirmed via `dbt compile`.

lessons.title: dbt_utils: The Macros You'll Actually Reuse

slots.practicalActivity: Add `dbt-labs/dbt_utils` to packages.yml, run `dbt deps`, then use at least one real dbt_utils macro in a model — `dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key()` to build a surrogate key on a mart, or `dbt_utils.date_spine()` to build a date table.
slots.deliverable: A packages.yml declaring dbt_utils, with at least one model successfully using a real dbt_utils macro, confirmed via `dbt run`.

slots.practicalActivity: Initialize a real Git repository for your dbt project (or confirm one already exists) with a proper .gitignore covering target/ and dbt_packages/, push it to GitHub, then either enable dbt Cloud's 'Run on Pull Requests' CI job or write a minimal GitHub Actions workflow that runs `dbt build` on every pull request.
slots.deliverable: A dbt project in a real GitHub repository with a working CI check (dbt Cloud job or GitHub Actions workflow) that runs on pull requests.

lessons.title: Slim CI: Only Running What Changed

slots.practicalActivity: If you have dbt Cloud access, create a scheduled production job (e.g. daily `dbt build`) and a separate CI job configured with 'defer to a previous run' state comparison for Slim CI; otherwise, document the exact job settings you'd configure for each. Open a pull request that touches only one model and confirm (or reason through) that Slim CI builds only that model and its downstream dependents.
slots.deliverable: A configured (or fully documented) dbt Cloud production job and Slim CI job, with evidence or reasoning that a one-model change triggers a build of only that model's changed subgraph.

slots.practicalActivity: Set up at least two dbt targets/environments (e.g. dev and prod) with different schemas in profiles.yml or dbt Cloud environment settings, then run `dbt run --target dev` followed by `dbt run --target prod` and confirm in Snowflake that each built into its own separate schema.
slots.deliverable: Two confirmed, separate schemas in Snowflake (dev and prod) produced by running the same project against two different dbt targets.

slots.practicalActivity: CI/CD drill: open a pull request with one deliberately broken model (a typo'd ref() or a test that will fail), watch your CI job catch it with a real red X, fix the break in a new commit on the same branch, and confirm the same PR goes green before merging it to main.
slots.deliverable: A single pull request with a documented failing CI run followed by a passing CI run after a fix, merged to main.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a `semantic_models` YAML block for one of your marts, naming at least one entity, one dimension, and one measure, then add a `type: simple` metric on top of that measure with a filter excluding at least one category of row (e.g. cancelled orders).
slots.deliverable: A semantic_models + metrics YAML block that compiles cleanly, with the metric's filter logic written out and explained in a one-sentence comment.

slots.practicalActivity: Query your Chapter 5 snapshot table directly and write a SELECT that reconstructs 'what did this row look like on date X' using the snapshot's dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to columns, then add one data-quality pattern of your own choosing (a freshness check on a source, or a not_null test on a previously untested column).
slots.deliverable: A point-in-time SCD Type 2 query against your snapshot table, plus one new data-quality check added to the project and passing in `dbt test`.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Raw Data to Reporting

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm your three raw sources are queryable in Snowflake (reuse the Snowflake course capstone's raw schema, or land three sources of similarly different shapes now), initialize a real Git repository for this capstone project, and write one sentence each on your fact model's grain and which two staging sources your intermediate model will combine — before writing a single .sql file.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed-queryable set of 3 raw sources, a new Git repository for the capstone, and a written one-sentence grain/join plan for the fact model.

slots.practicalActivity: Define sources.yml for all three raw sources with a freshness check on at least one, build one staging model per source, then build at least one intermediate model combining two or more of them — exactly the order of operations the capstone brief lays out, before touching marts.
slots.deliverable: A sources.yml with a freshness check, 3 staging models (one per source), and 1 intermediate model, all building cleanly via `dbt run`.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the marts layer (at least one fact and one dimension model), add generic tests on every key column plus one singular test encoding a business rule, write full schema.yml descriptions for every mart-layer model and column, and generate a real dbt Docs site showing the whole lineage graph. Then add history and incremental refresh: a snapshot capturing slowly changing history on at least one dimension, at least one mart converted to `materialized='incremental'` instead of a full rebuild every run, and at least one dbt_utils macro (a surrogate key is the natural fit) somewhere in the project.
slots.deliverable: A complete marts layer with a green `dbt test` run, a generated dbt Docs site, one working snapshot, one incremental mart, and at least one dbt_utils macro in active use, all confirmed with real builds.

slots.practicalActivity: Put the whole capstone project in Git with meaningful commit messages across multiple commits (not one giant commit), push it to GitHub, then connect Power BI (or another BI tool) to your marts layer through a view tuned for BI consumption rather than exposing the raw marts tables as-is.
slots.deliverable: A capstone project pushed to GitHub with a real commit history, plus a BI tool successfully connected and querying your marts layer.

slots.practicalActivity: Walk a stranger (a peer, mentor, or yourself on a recording) through the whole capstone project end to end — the raw sources, the staging/intermediate/marts layering decisions, the tests and docs, the snapshot and incremental model, and the connected BI tool — then write down 2 things you'd improve with more time.
slots.deliverable: A completed capstone walkthrough (live or recorded) covering every layer of the project, plus a written list of 2 concrete 'v2' improvements, ready to add to a portfolio.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can take raw tables already landed in a warehouse and build a real, tested, documented, version-controlled dbt project — sources, staging, intermediate and marts models, generic and singular tests, snapshots, incremental models, macros, and a CI-checked pull-request workflow — that a BI tool can query directly.
